source.title: The Signs Were Always There: Training-Free Detection and Control in Raw Transformer Dimensions
source.authors: V. Nalagatla; Madhavi Evana; Yi-Wen Zhang

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures whether concepts are detectable from individual FFN neuron-activation signs, a related but different test from counting neuron poles with one or more named jobs.
record.gate_note: Table 18 reports sign-based concept-detection results in FFN neuron activations. It does not estimate the share of poles with one or two jobs, test neuron explanations against unseen activating examples, or score model-generated neuron explanations. The residual-stream and other results do not measure those version-specific outcomes.
record.test_reason: No version is tested. The paper reads concepts from individual residual, attention and FFN dimensions by sign agreement against 175 curated concepts. It never assigns jobs to neuron poles or counts how many neurons have one or two jobs, so V1 and V2 are not tested. It does not study InceptionV1 (V3), vision-model interpretable shares or tool effects (V4), neuron attribution graphs (V5), held-out tests of neuron explanations (V6), or simulation scoring (V7). It argues that real transformers are axis-aligned and that superposition pressure does not bind. That is the essay's theme, but measured through a different construct. Appendix K's FFN-neuron AUCs give per-concept detectability, not per-neuron job shares. The record's 'tests/T2' is therefore wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase covers only Appendix K. The authors' overall conclusion is broader. Individual dimensions act as binary registers, with signs carrying content and magnitudes carrying strength. This allows training-free concept discovery, detection and control across language, vision and audio. They hold that this shifts the problem from finding a rotation to cataloging dimensions, while not refuting superposition. The Appendix K FFN results are explicitly correlational.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses Bag-of-Dims sign-based concept detection on individual activation dimensions, rather than auditing poles by assigning and validating named neuron-job explanations.
record.method_sensitivity: The neuron-activation measurements are reported at the selected three-quarters-depth layer for each model; no neuron-pole job-share sensitivity analysis is reported.

fits_no_version.finding: FFN neuron activation signs support sign-based detection of curated concepts at levels similar to the residual stream: feature AUC 0.973–0.994, with 165–175 of 175 concepts above null across four models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concept information is sign-readable from individual FFN neuron activations, without establishing that each neuron has one main job.

fits_no_version.finding: Pairwise sign mutual information between residual dimensions is below 0.006 bits, and an MLP adds nothing over axis-aligned logistic regression. In a toy model, superposition coupling falls as the bottleneck relaxes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Real transformer residual dimensions are functionally axis-aligned, and the superposition regime may not bind in practice (related to the theme of V3/V4, but not measured on neurons or InceptionV1).

record.problems: The neuron analysis uses a curated set of 175 concepts and reports detection scores rather than independently validated named jobs or pole-level job shares. The authors explicitly state that these activation-space measurements are correlational and do not establish neurons as causal writers of concepts.
record.rows_left_out: No further neuron-activation results in Table 18 were omitted; residual-stream values are included as the stated reference baselines. Other paper results do not report pole-level job counts or tests of neuron explanations.

untested.parts: All: no count of Qwen3-32B neuron poles by number of jobs.
All: no neuron job-share estimates in any model; scale tested only up to 32B.
All: no InceptionV1 or classic polysemantic neuron analysis.
All: no interpretable-neuron share in vision CNNs and no tool or architecture comparison.
All: no held-out test of neuron explanations.
All: no simulation-based scoring of explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's verdict that no version is tested is right, but 'tests/T2' contradicts it. Reclassified as discusses/T6. Rows are kept as context only.

versions.untested_parts: Does not count Qwen3-32B neuron poles by number of jobs or report the claimed 90%, 7%, and 2–4% shares.
Does not estimate pole job-count shares across models or test scaling up to trillions of parameters.
Does not examine InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons or test the proposed pose/recursive-generalization account.
Does not estimate interpretable-neuron shares in InceptionV1-sized vision models or test the proposed architecture, regularization, and tool explanation.
Does not test whether attribution graphs built from a model's own neurons explain behavior without a replacement model.
Does not test explanations of individual neurons against held-out activations or measure whether explanations that fit activating examples fail to predict firing.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating their predicted activations on new text.

rows.subject: Qwen 3.5-4B
rows.operation_detail: Measured per-dimension sign-based concept detection in FFN neuron activations.

conditions.value: same 50-anchor concept set; 171 concepts for Mistral only

rows.measure: Per-dimension max AUC for neuron activations
rows.note: The paper also reports neuron feature AUC 0.990 versus residual 0.983 and 175/175 concepts exceeding null. These concept-detection metrics do not give a count of neuron poles by number of jobs.
rows.check: Per-dim max AUC is the best single neuron per concept, a selection statistic over neurons, not a share of neurons with one job.
